chunks: Flip-flop versus latch. The question: What is the difference between a flip-flop and latch?
Both a latch and a flip-flop store one bit, but they listen to their input differently.
A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable (a control input) is active, its output follows its input, and when the enable goes inactive it holds the last value.
A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it looks at its input only at the instant of a clock edge and ignores everything else. A flip-flop is built from two latches.
Think of a single door versus an airlock. A single door, the latch, lets anything through while it is open, so whatever happens outside is visible inside.
An airlock has two doors that are never open together. That is a flip-flop. Items advance one step per cycle, and there is never a straight path from outside to inside.
One thing the picture hides: the airlock's doors swap at a single instant, the clock edge, so only that instant's input counts.
Each clock period is four slots. The latch (orange) is transparent while CLK is high: in the first high phase, D is 1 then 0, and Q follows both.
The flip-flop (blue) only samples D at each rising edge: at the first edge D just before the edge is 1, so Q goes to 1 and stays until the next edge, ignoring D's change in between.
Latch: a storage element that is transparent while its enable is active, then holds. Flip-flop: a storage element that samples its input only at a clock edge.
Transparent: the output follows the input, so any change or glitch (a brief false blip) passes straight through.
Master-slave: two latches in series that open on opposite clock phases, forming a flip-flop.
Inferred latch: an accidental latch created when hardware code leaves a signal unassigned in some branch.
Feed the same signals to both. The clock rises, and D is 1 at that moment. Later, while the clock is still high, D falls to 0.
The latch is transparent, so its output goes to 1 and then follows D down to 0, changing twice in one period.
The flip-flop sampled D only at the rising edge, so its output goes to 1 and stays there until the next edge.
"A latch is level-sensitive: it's transparent while its enable is active and holds when it isn't.
A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D at one clock edge and ignores the input otherwise.
A flip-flop is two latches in series, master and slave, with opposite clock phases, so there's never a transparent path from D to Q.
Flip-flops give simple, predictable timing; latches are smaller and allow time borrowing but pass glitches and are trickier to analyze."
